IG: Brent oil falls 4 percent on Iran deal hopes
Benzinga: Crude oil choppy as Strait of Hormuz flows fall

more.h: Background: why oil matters to central banks
more.p: Oil prices feed into inflation directly through petrol and diesel, and indirectly through transport and production costs. Central banks cannot control oil, but they worry when high prices push up inflation expectations. In Australia, fuel was cited in October CPI previews, with an 8.5% rise in fuel prices expected by Shane Oliver, and the RBA's Bullock named elevated oil prices as an upside risk to inflation.

Coverage I found says Brent ended the most recent week at $92.58, down 21% from its October high, after dropping to a low of $89.23. Prices fell on reports of diplomatic progress and rose when Iran's top security official denied that any talks with Washington were under way, with one report describing a rise of almost 3% to around $94. The EIA's November outlook, released on 10 November, expects Brent to average about $100 in November and December, $97 for 2026 and $86 in 2027. Shipping attacks in the Strait of Hormuz remain a source of volatility. The weekly dates on these items are relative, so exact prices will have moved.

more.h: Different views and what it means
more.p:
Analysts note that a sustained fall driven by easing supply risk would help oil-importing economies by lowering energy and transport costs and easing inflation pressure, which is the logic behind Westpac's lower-oil-price argument that rates have peaked. But the history of the past fortnight is that headlines reverse quickly, and a rebound is possible if the crisis escalates.

For your market literacy, oil is a good example of a variable that sets the macro narrative: it touches inflation, the Australian dollar (via the terms of trade) and bank credit through fuel-intensive sectors such as transport and agriculture.
October CPI on Wednesday 25 November will show fuel's contribution, and the RBA decides on 8 December. I did not find verified dates for any US-Iran talks.

primer.text: A fall of at least 10% from a recent peak. It is milder than a bear market (20% or more) and is a normal part of market cycles, but a fast one can unsettle investors.
A central bank telling markets in advance what it is likely to do with rates. It reduces surprises but can box the bank in, which is why the Fed's new Chair is trying to limit it.
The profit and loss cost of loans that have gone bad or are expected to. It has a specific part for troubled customers and a collective part based on the bank's economic forecast.
China's benchmark lending rate, published monthly. The one-year rate prices most business loans and the five-year rate anchors mortgages.

quiz.q: The S&P 500 'entered a correction' on Friday 20 November. What does that mean?
options: It fell at least 10% from a recent peak
It fell 20% or more from a peak
Trading was halted for the day
quiz.explain: A correction is a fall of at least 10% from a recent high. A fall of 20% or more is usually called a bear market.

quiz.q: NAB's FY26 credit impairment charge rose to about $1.5bn mainly because of what?
options: Provisions for specific troubled customers and a forward-looking top-up for a weaker economy
A fall in home loan volumes
quiz.explain: About $1.1bn came from individually assessed customers and about $464m from collective forward-looking provisions, with business lending the main pressure point.

quiz.q: What did the PBOC do with China's loan prime rates on 20 November?
options: Left them at 3.0% (one-year) and 3.5% (five-year) for an 18th month
quiz.explain: Both rates were unchanged for the 18th straight month, even as the PBOC shifted its policy rate to the overnight reverse repo rate.

quiz.q: From 1 July 2026, how must employers pay the super guarantee under Payday Super?
options: At the same time as wages
quiz.explain: Payday Super requires super to be paid at the same time as wages rather than quarterly, to speed up contributions and cut unpaid super.

markets.summary: A global AI-led sell-off dominated: the S&P 500 fell 3.7% on Friday to enter a correction, the ASX 200 lost 5.39% on the week (its worst since June 2022), and the Australian dollar slid to about 0.663 US cents, its lowest since December 2025. Markets have priced out most of a December RBA hike, while a US hike is seen as near certain.
markets.forWestpac: Westpac fell about 2.2% on Friday, the most of the big four. The bank's economists expect an RBA hold on 8 December, but Wednesday's October CPI and rising arrears commentary from the big four keep credit quality and margins in focus.
